A video circulating on social media alleges that the first woman to be vaccinated in Presidente Figueiredo, a municipality in the state of Amazonas, Brazil, did not actually receive an injection during her COVID-19 vaccination. The clip has fueled skepticism about the integrity of the local vaccination campaign and has prompted concerns about vaccine administration practices.

The claim centers on footage that appears to show a healthcare worker preparing to administer the vaccine to an elderly woman, identified as the first recipient in the region’s immunization effort. Observers on social media argue that the syringe in the video seems to be empty or that the plunger was not pressed, suggesting that the woman did not receive the intended dose.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to examine the context in which the video was recorded and to analyze the visual evidence presented.

First, the video in question was reportedly captured during a public event designed to launch the vaccination rollout in Presidente Figueiredo. Such events are often documented by local authorities and the media to promote transparency and to encourage vaccine uptake among the broader population.

Upon review, the footage shows the nurse inserting the needle into the woman’s upper arm. Some viewers claim that the nurse does not visibly depress the plunger, leading to speculation that no vaccine was administered. However, the video quality, camera angle, and the brief nature of the recording make it difficult to conclusively determine whether the injection was properly given.

Healthcare professionals have noted that in some cases, syringes used for vaccinations have transparent barrels, and depending on lighting and video resolution, the liquid may not be clearly visible. Moreover, the process of administering a vaccine can be quick, and the plunger movement may be subtle, especially if the dose is small.

In response to similar allegations in other parts of Brazil, local health authorities have reiterated protocols to ensure correct vaccine administration, including the requirement that syringes be shown to cameras and recipients before and after the injection. In some cases, authorities have conducted internal investigations and, if errors were identified, have offered revaccination to affected individuals.

As for the specific case in Presidente Figueiredo, there is no official confirmation from local health authorities that the woman did not receive her vaccine. Without additional footage or testimony from those present, it is not possible to definitively state that the injection did not occur. The available evidence is inconclusive, and the claim remains unproven.

While skepticism and vigilance regarding public health procedures are important, it is also essential to avoid drawing firm conclusions from ambiguous video evidence. To maintain public trust, health authorities should continue to prioritize transparent communication and strict adherence to vaccination protocols.

सामाजिक सञ्जालमा प्रसारित एउटा भिडियो अभियोग लगाइएको छ कि ब्राजीलको अमेज़नास राज्यमा बसोबास गर्ने एउटा महानगर प्रेसिडेन्ट फिगेरेडोमा आई. विक्षेप लिने पहिलो महिला को खाली इंजेक्सन छैन। भिडियो क्लिपले स्थानीय वैक्सीन अभियानको सत्यता मा संदेह बढाएको छ र वैक्सीन प्रशासन विधिको चिन्ता उत्पन्न गरेको छ।

अभियोग भिडियो छानामा केन्द्रित छ जसले एउटा स्वास्थ्य कर्मचारीले एउटा वृद्ध महिलाको वैक्सीन दिन तयार भएको देखिन्छ जसलाई क्षेत्रको इम्युनाइजेशन अभियानको पहिलो प्राप्तकर्ता भएको छ। सामाजिक सञ्जालमा अवलोकनकर्ता भन्छन् कि भिडियोमा इंजेक्सन छोरा खाली देखिन्छ वा प्लंगर दबाइएको छैन, जसले महिलाले आवश्यक डोज प्राप्त गरेको छैन भन्दै छ।

यो अभियोगको सत्यता जाँच गर्न आवश्यक छ जसले भिडियो रेकर्ड गरिएको संदर्भ र दृश्य आधारित प्रमाणको विश्लेषण गर्न आवश्यक छ। पहिलो, भिडियोले सार्वजनिक घटनामा रेकर्ड गरिएको छ जसले प्रेसिडेन्ट फिगेरेडोमा वैक्सीन अभियान शुरु गर्नका लागि डिज़ाइन गरिएको छ। जस्ता घटनाहरू स्थानीय अधिकारीहरू र मिडियाले अपारदर्शिता बढाउन र जनताको बर्बाद जनसंख्यामा वैक्सीन लिन उत्साहित गर्नका लागि रेकर्ड गरिएको छ।

समीक्षा गर्दा भिडियोले नर्सले महिलाको उपरी आँगालमा छोरा लगाउने देखिन्छ। केही प्रेक्षकहरू भन्छन् कि नर्सले प्लंगर दबाउन देखिन्छ छैन, जसले अनुमान छ कि कुनै वैक्सीन दिइएको छैन। तथापि, भिडियो गुणवत्ता, केमेरा कोण र छोटो आवृत्ति भिडियोले इंजेक्सन ठीक दिइएको छ वा छैन भन्न निर्णय गर्न गाह्रो छ।

स्वास्थ्य विशेषज्ञहरूले ध्यान दिएको छ कि केही मामलामा वैक्सीन लिन उपयोग गरिएका सिरिंजहरू पारदर्शी छोरा हुन्छन् र प्रकाश र भिडियो छाना अनुसार तरल भने धेरै स्पष्ट देखिन सक्छ। त्यस्तै, वैक्सीन दिन क्रम त्वरित हुन सक्छ र प्लंगरको गति सूक्ष्म हुन सक्छ, विशेष गरी यदि डोज छोटो हुन छ।

अन्य स्थानहरूमा समान आरोपहरूको जवाबमा स्थानीय स्वास्थ्य अधिकारीहरूले प्रोटोकॉलहरू पुनरावर्तन गरेको छ, जसमा सिरिंजहरू केमेरा र प्राप्तकर्ताहरूलाई इंजेक्सन अगाडि र पछि देखाइएको आवश्यकता छ। केही मामलामा, अधिकारीहरूले आंतरिक अनुसन्धान गरेको छ र यदि त्रुटि चिनियो भए त आवेदक व्यक्तिहरूलाई पुनः वैक्सीन लिन आफ्नो प्रस्ताव गरेको छ।

प्रेसिडेन्ट फिगेरेडोमा विशेष मामला बारे, स्थानीय स्वास्थ्य अधिकारीहरूले महिलाले आफ्नो वैक्सीन प्राप्त गरेको छैन भन्ने आधिकारिक पुष्टि छैन। उपस्थित व्यक्तिहरूको अतिरिक्त छाना वा घोषणा बिना, इंजेक्सन भएको छैन भन्ने निश्चित रूपमा बताउन सम्भव छैन। उपलब्ध प्रमाण अस्पष्ट छ र अभियोग अप्रमाणित छ।

जनताको स्वास्थ्य प्रक्रियामा संदेह र निगरानी आवश्यक छ, तर अस्पष्ट भिडियो प्रमाणबाट ठाउँ निश्चित गर्न आवश्यक छ। जनताको भरोसा बनाउन, स्वास्थ्य अधिकारीहरूले अपारदर्शी संचार र वैक्सीन अभियानको कठोर अनुसरण जारी राख्न आवश्यक छ।

A social media post circulating online claims that Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, son of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and João Doria, former governor of São Paulo, conspired to buy stocks from Sinovac, a major Chinese pharmaceutical company. The post further alleges that Fábio Lula da Silva now owns 20% of Sinovac. This article examines the context, background, and veracity of these claims.

**Background and Context**

Sinovac Biotech is a Chinese biopharmaceutical company best known in Brazil for developing the CoronaVac COVID-19 vaccine. During the pandemic, the state of São Paulo, under then-governor João Doria, partnered with Sinovac to produce and distribute CoronaVac in Brazil through the Instituto Butantan, a respected biomedical research center.

Fábio Luís Lula da Silva, commonly known as Lulinha, is the eldest son of President Lula. Lulinha has been the subject of various rumors and allegations regarding his business activities, but there is no public record of him being involved in the pharmaceutical sector, nor of any official business connection with Sinovac.

João Doria, as governor, was a prominent figure in securing vaccines for São Paulo and Brazil, often positioning himself in opposition to the federal government’s slower vaccine rollout. His actions were politically significant, but there have been no credible reports linking him personally to the ownership or acquisition of Sinovac shares.

**Analysis of the Claims**

The claim can be broken down into three core components: (1) a conspiracy between Lulinha and Doria to buy Sinovac stocks, (2) the purchase of Sinovac stocks by Lulinha, and (3) Lulinha now owning 20% of Sinovac.

First, there is no evidence of any conspiracy or secret agreement between Fábio Lula da Silva and João Doria regarding Sinovac stocks. Their public roles and statements have not indicated any business partnership or shared financial interest in the company.

Second, the assertion that Fábio Lula da Silva acquired Sinovac stocks cannot be substantiated. Sinovac is a Chinese company, and its major shareholding structure does not include any disclosures of ownership by Brazilian individuals or entities, especially not by Lulinha. International share purchases of such magnitude would be subject to regulatory filings and likely receive significant media attention, neither of which have occurred.

Third, the claim that Lulinha owns 20% of Sinovac is implausible. As a publicly traded company, Sinovac’s ownership structure is a matter of public record. No public information supports the notion that a Brazilian national, let alone Lulinha, holds such a large stake. Such ownership would make him one of the company’s largest shareholders, a fact that would be readily verifiable and widely reported.

**Conclusion**

After careful examination, the claims in the social media post are unfounded. There is no evidence that Fábio Lula da Silva and João Doria conspired to buy Sinovac stocks, nor is there any indication that Lulinha owns 20% of the company. The post appears to be based on misinformation, conflating political rivalries and vaccine-related controversies with unsupported allegations of personal financial gain. Readers should be cautious about accepting such claims without credible evidence.

A recent social media post claims that Brazilian actress Fernanda Torres stated she hoped COVID-19 would help “eliminate” supporters of former President Jair Bolsonaro. This assertion, if true, would suggest a high-profile public figure expressing a wish for harm against a segment of the Brazilian population. Given the controversial nature of such a statement, it is important to examine the origins of this claim, the context of any relevant comments by Fernanda Torres, and whether the actress actually made such a declaration.

Fernanda Torres is a well-known Brazilian actress, writer, and social commentator, recognized both for her roles in film and television and for her published essays and columns in national media. She has been an outspoken critic of Jair Bolsonaro, particularly regarding his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic. Bolsonaro, who served as Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2022, faced widespread criticism domestically and internationally for his approach to the pandemic, including downplaying the severity of COVID-19, resisting lockdown measures, and promoting unproven treatments.

The claim that Torres hoped the pandemic would “eliminate” Bolsonaro’s supporters appears to have originated from a misinterpretation and subsequent viral spread of comments she made in a 2020 essay. In May 2020, Torres wrote a column reflecting on the polarization in Brazil during the pandemic. In her piece, she expressed frustration with the political divide and the behavior of Bolsonaro’s base in resisting public health measures. However, at no point did she state or imply that she wished harm or death upon Bolsonaro’s supporters.

Instead, Torres critiqued the political landscape and lamented the consequences of misinformation, particularly how it affected public adherence to health guidelines. The phrase “eliminate Bolsonaro’s supporters” does not appear in her writings or public statements. The misattribution seems to stem from a passage where she commented on the possibility that the pandemic might “expose the fallacies” of certain political beliefs or reveal the dangers of denying science—not a hope that the virus would physically harm specific individuals.

Fact-checking previous interviews and public appearances by Fernanda Torres reinforces this analysis. While she has been a vocal opponent of Bolsonaro’s policies and rhetoric, she has consistently framed her criticism in terms of political and social consequences, not personal animosity or calls for violence. There is no documented instance of Torres expressing a desire for COVID-19 to “eliminate” anyone, including Bolsonaro’s supporters.

The social media post in question appears to be an example of misinformation, taking a public figure’s critical remarks out of context and exaggerating them for sensational effect. Such distortions can contribute to further polarization and misunderstanding, particularly in the fraught political climate surrounding COVID-19 and its aftermath in Brazil.

In summary, the claim that Fernanda Torres said she hoped COVID-19 would eliminate Bolsonaro’s supporters is not supported by any verifiable evidence. Torres has criticized Bolsonaro and his base, but there is no record of her expressing a wish for harm against his supporters. The statement circulating on social media is false and a misrepresentation of her public comments.

Claims circulating on social media have stated that the Brazilian state of Amapá has officially adopted an “early treatment” protocol for COVID-19 and, as a result, now boasts the lowest lethality rates in the world. This assertion has sparked considerable discussion, particularly among groups advocating for the use of off-label medications in the treatment of COVID-19. A closer examination of this claim reveals several important factors to consider, including the actual public health policies in Amapá, the definition and reliability of “early treatment” protocols, and the statistics regarding COVID-19 lethality rates.

To begin, Amapá is a small state in northern Brazil, notable for its remote location and relatively low population density compared to other Brazilian states. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Amapá, like other regions of Brazil, faced significant challenges, including overloaded hospitals and limited access to medical resources at various points during the health crisis.

The concept of “early treatment” for COVID-19 in Brazil has generally referred to the use of medications such as hydroxychloroquine, ivermectin, azithromycin, and others, often administered to patients shortly after a positive diagnosis in hopes of preventing severe illness. This approach gained traction in some Brazilian municipalities and among certain groups despite the lack of conclusive scientific evidence supporting its effectiveness. The World Health Organization and major health authorities have repeatedly stated that these drugs are not proven to prevent severe COVID-19 outcomes and, in some cases, may carry risks of side effects.

Regarding Amapá’s official protocols, while there have been reports of some municipalities or individual doctors recommending or providing off-label medications as “early treatment,” there is no evidence that the state government of Amapá has formally adopted a universal “early treatment” policy as a matter of public health. State health authorities have generally followed broader national guidelines, which have evolved over time in response to new scientific data and recommendations from Brazil’s Ministry of Health.

The claim that Amapá has “the lowest lethality rates in the world” also requires scrutiny. COVID-19 lethality rates, typically calculated as the number of deaths divided by the number of confirmed cases, can vary widely depending on factors such as population demographics, testing capacity, reporting practices, and access to healthcare. While Amapá’s lethality rate has at times been lower than the national Brazilian average, there is no verifiable evidence that it holds the lowest rate globally. Fluctuations in reported cases and deaths, differences in data collection, and the size of the population make it difficult to make accurate international comparisons, particularly with much larger or more populous regions.

In summary, the claim that Amapá has officially adopted an “early treatment” protocol as a statewide policy and, as a result, has achieved the lowest COVID-19 lethality rate in the world, is not supported by current evidence. While some elements of “early treatment” have been present in isolated cases, there is no formal, state-level policy, nor is there credible data confirming Amapá’s lethality rate is the lowest worldwide. Public health outcomes are influenced by a complex web of factors, and attributing low lethality rates to a single intervention oversimplifies a multifaceted issue.

Para magsimula, ang Amapá ay isang maliit na estado sa hilagang bahagi ng Brazil, kilala para sa kanyang malayong lokasyon at mas mababa na populasyon density kumpara sa iba pang mga estado sa Brazil. Sa panahon ng pandemya ng COVID-19, ang Amapá, tulad ng iba pang mga rehiyon sa Brazil, ay naging mahirap dahil sa mga kahinaan, tulad ng mga mapait na ospital at limitadong access sa mga medikal na recursos sa iba't ibang puntos ng krisis sa kalusugan.

Ang konsepto ng "maagang paggamot" para sa COVID-19 sa Brazil ay karaniwang tumutukoy sa paggamit ng mga gamot tulad ng hydroxychloroquine, ivermectin, azithromycin, at iba pa, na madalas inihahatid sa mga pasyente ngunit matapos ang positibo na diagnosis, sa pag-asa na mapanatili ang kahusayan. Ang paraan na ito ay naging popular sa ilang mga lungsod sa Brazil at sa ilang mga grupo, kahit walang konklusibong ebidensya na nagpapatunay sa epektibidad nito. Ang World Health Organization at mga pangunahing ahensya sa kalusugan ay nagsabi na ang mga gamot na ito ay hindi pa nakakatulong sa pag-iwas sa mapanganib na resulta ng COVID-19 at, sa ilang mga kaso, maaaring magdulot ng mga epekto ng side effects.

Sa kahilaian ng mga opisyales ng kalusugan ng estado ng Amapá, kahit may mga ulat na ang ilang mga lungsod o mga indibidwal na doktor ay nagsasabi o nagbibigay ng mga gamot na hindi nakalaan para sa paggamot bilang "maagang paggamot," walang ebidensya na ang pamahalaan ng estado ng Amapá ay nagsagawa ng isang pangkabug-os na "maagang paggamot" na polisiya bilang isang pangkalusugan. Ang mga opisyales ng kalusugan ng estado ay karaniwang sumusunod sa mga pangkabug-os na mga gabay ng bansa, na nagbabago sa panahon ayon sa mga bagong datos sa kalusugan at mga rekomendasyon mula sa Ministry of Health ng Brazil.

Ang pahayag na ang Amapá ay "may pinakamababang antas ng kamatayan sa mundo" ay nangangailangan ng mas matalinong pagsusuri. Ang mga antas ng kamatayan sa COVID-19, karaniwang isinasaalang-alang bilang ang bilang ng mga kamatayon ay hinahati sa bilang ng mga nakakatotohanang kaso, ay maaaring mag-iba-iba depende sa mga salik tulad ng demograhiya ng populasyon, kakayahang pagsusuri, mga paraan ng pagsusulat, at access sa kalusugan. Kahit ang antas ng kamatayan sa Amapá ay nangunguna sa average na antas ng bansa sa ilang mga panahon, walang nakakatotohanang ebidensya na ito ay ang pinakamababang antas sa buong mundo. Ang mga pagbabago sa mga nakakatotohanang kaso at kamatayon, ang mga pagkakaiba sa pagkakatulungan ng data, at ang bilang ng populasyon ay nagdudulot ng kakaiba sa pagmamaneho ng mga akurat na pag-uugnay sa pandaigdigan, lalo na sa mga rehiyon na mas malaki o may mas malaking populasyon.

Sa kabuuan, ang pahayag na ang Amapá ay nagsagawa ng isang opisyales na "maagang paggamot" na polisiya bilang isang estado at bilang resulta, ito ay nangunguna sa mga antas ng kamatayan ng COVID-19 sa mundo ay hindi nakakatulong ngayon sa mga ebidensya. Kahit ang ilang mga elemento ng "maagang paggamot" ay nasa ilang mga kaso, walang opisyales, estado-antas na polisiya, at walang nakakatotohanang data na nagpapatunay na ang antas ng kamatayan ng Amapá ay ang pinakamababang sa buong mundo. Ang mga resulta ng kalusugan ng publiko ay nakaapekto ng isang komplikadong network ng mga salik, at ang pag-ugnay ng mababang antas ng kamatayan sa isang solong interbensyon ay nagdudulot ng simpleng pag-unawa sa isang kompleks na isyu.

In recent years, debates around the effectiveness of hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) as a treatment for COVID-19 have gained significant traction, fueled by social media posts and public figures. A recent post on social media claims: “The Lancet retracted an article that state hydroxychloroquine is ineffective against COVID-19. Thus, it is effective.” This assertion draws a direct line between the retraction of a high-profile scientific article and the purported effectiveness of HCQ against COVID-19. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to understand the context of the retracted article, the reasons for its withdrawal, and the broader body of scientific evidence regarding HCQ and COVID-19.

Background on The Lancet Retraction

In May 2020, The Lancet, one of the world’s leading medical journals, published a large observational study suggesting that hydroxychloroquine and chloroquine were not only ineffective against COVID-19 but potentially associated with increased mortality and heart complications in hospitalized patients. This study had a substantial impact, influencing public policy and the suspension of several clinical trials globally.

However, soon after publication, independent researchers raised concerns about the validity of the data used in the study. Questions emerged about the integrity and provenance of the database managed by the company Surgisphere, which provided the patient data. The inability of the authors to provide access to the full dataset for independent verification led The Lancet to retract the article in June 2020, citing concerns over data reliability.

Does the Retraction Prove HCQ is Effective?

The social media claim concludes that, because the article showing HCQ was ineffective was retracted, this means the drug is effective. This interpretation misunderstands the nature of scientific retractions and the scientific process. A retraction means that the evidence provided in that particular study cannot be relied upon—it does not mean that the opposite claim (in this case, that HCQ is effective) is thereby proven. Retraction is a corrective measure for flawed or unverifiable research, not a reversal of the findings.

The Broader Evidence on Hydroxychloroquine

Since the start of the pandemic, hydroxychloroquine has been studied in numerous randomized controlled trials and observational studies. The initial excitement over its potential was based on laboratory studies and small early clinical reports. However, as larger, well-designed clinical trials were conducted, the consensus among the scientific and medical community shifted. Most rigorous studies have found that hydroxychloroquine, whether used alone or in combination with other drugs, does not significantly reduce mortality or improve clinical outcomes in COVID-19 patients. In some cases, safety concerns have also been documented, particularly regarding cardiac side effects.

Conclusion

While The Lancet did retract a high-profile article on hydroxychloroquine and COVID-19 due to issues with data reliability, this does not equate to evidence that hydroxychloroquine is effective against COVID-19. The retraction indicates only that the specific study’s data and conclusions are unreliable, not that the opposite is true. The overall scientific consensus, based on multiple high-quality studies, is that hydroxychloroquine is not an effective treatment for COVID-19. Social media users should be cautious in drawing sweeping conclusions from retractions or isolated studies without considering the broader body of scientific evidence.

A social media post has recently circulated, claiming that President Joe Biden stated hydroxychloroquine is effective against COVID-19 and that the media refused to criticize him for it. This claim warrants close scrutiny, given the ongoing public debate over hydroxychloroquine and the heightened attention to political statements regarding COVID-19 treatments.

Hydroxychloroquine, an antimalarial and autoimmune disease medication, gained widespread attention during the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic. In 2020, some public figures, including then-President Donald Trump, promoted hydroxychloroquine as a potential treatment for COVID-19. However, subsequent studies and statements from health authorities such as the Food and Drug Administration and the World Health Organization concluded that hydroxychloroquine was not effective in treating COVID-19 and could, in some cases, carry significant risks.

The core assertion of the social media post is that Joe Biden publicly endorsed the effectiveness of hydroxychloroquine against COVID-19. A thorough review of public statements, interviews, press conferences, and official communications from Joe Biden, both during his 2020 presidential campaign and throughout his presidency, reveals no record of him making such a claim. On the contrary, Biden has repeatedly called for reliance on scientific expertise and evidence-based treatments in response to the pandemic. His administration has consistently deferred to the guidance of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other public health agencies regarding COVID-19 treatments.

Given this context, the first part of the social media post is inaccurate. There is no documented instance in which Joe Biden stated hydroxychloroquine is effective against COVID-19. In fact, he has often criticized the promotion of unproven remedies and emphasized vaccination as the primary strategy for combating the virus.

The second part of the claim alleges that the media refused to criticize Biden for his supposed statement. Media coverage of COVID-19 treatments has been extensive and, at times, highly critical of political leaders who endorse unproven therapies. During the period when hydroxychloroquine was a topic of public discourse, media outlets scrutinized politicians’ statements and quickly reported on any misinformation. If Biden had made such a remark, it is likely that major news organizations would have reported on it, given their pattern of coverage in similar situations. Instead, the media coverage related to Biden has focused largely on his administration’s efforts to increase vaccine availability, distribute personal protective equipment, and address the pandemic with guidance from scientists and medical experts.

In summary, the claim that Joe Biden has stated hydroxychloroquine is effective against COVID-19 is not supported by evidence. There is no public record of him making such a statement, and his approach has been consistently aligned with scientific consensus. The suggestion that the media failed to criticize him for this alleged statement is also unfounded, as there is no documented incident to prompt such criticism. This social media post misrepresents Biden’s position and the media’s response, contributing to misinformation about the public discourse on COVID-19 treatments.

В заключение, твърдението, че Джо Байдън е изтъкнал, че хидроксихлорохинът е ефективно средство срещу ковид-19, не е подкрепено от доказателства. A recent social media post claims that “The United States are officially recommending hydroxychloroquine against COVID-19.” This statement suggests that the U.S. government has endorsed the use of hydroxychloroquine as an official treatment for COVID-19. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the U.S. federal government’s current recommendations, the scientific background of hydroxychloroquine in COVID-19 treatment, and recent policy developments.

Hydroxychloroquine is a medication traditionally used to prevent and treat malaria, as well as certain autoimmune diseases such as lupus and rheumatoid arthritis. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, hydroxychloroquine drew international attention as a potential treatment for the novel coronavirus. Initial laboratory studies showed some activity of the drug against the virus that causes COVID-19, and anecdotal reports suggested possible benefits. This led to emergency use authorizations (EUAs) in some countries, including the United States.

However, as the pandemic progressed, more rigorous clinical trials were conducted to evaluate the safety and efficacy of hydroxychloroquine in treating COVID-19. Multiple large-scale studies and randomized controlled trials ultimately demonstrated that hydroxychloroquine did not provide a significant benefit in reducing the severity, duration, or mortality of COVID-19. Some studies also highlighted potential risks, including serious cardiac side effects.

As a result of this evidence, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) revoked its emergency use authorization for hydroxychloroquine in June 2020, stating that the drug was unlikely to be effective in treating COVID-19 and that its risks outweighed potential benefits. Since then, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have not recommended hydroxychloroquine for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. The drug is not included in official treatment guidelines for the disease.

In the years since the revocation, there have been no reversals or new endorsements by major U.S. health agencies regarding hydroxychloroquine as a recommended treatment for COVID-19. While some individual practitioners and advocacy groups continue to promote its use, these views do not reflect official U.S. policy. Current federal guidelines emphasize the use of treatments such as antiviral medications (for example, Paxlovid) and monoclonal antibodies, depending on patient eligibility and the stage of illness.

In summary, the claim that “The United States are officially recommending hydroxychloroquine against COVID-19” is inaccurate. Federal agencies, including the FDA, CDC, and NIH, do not recommend the use of hydroxychloroquine for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19. The official guidance is based on extensive scientific research, which has found the drug to be ineffective for this purpose and potentially harmful. As of now, hydroxychloroquine should not be used for COVID-19 treatment except in the context of approved clinical trials.

આ પુરાવાને કારણે, યુનાઇટેડ સ્ટેટ્સ ફૂડ એન્ડ ડ્રગ એડમિનિસ્ટ્રેશન (FDA) એ હાઇડ્રોક્સીક્લોર્ક્વિનની આંતરિક ઉપયોગની મંજૂરી જૂન 2020માં રદ કરી હતી, જે દર્શાવ્યું હતું કે ઔષધિ કોવિડ-19 ઉપચારમાં અસરકારક હોઈ શકતી નથી અને તેના જોખમો તેના સંભવિત ફાયદાઓથી વધુ છે. ત્યારથી, યુનાઇટેડ સ્ટેટ્સ સેન્ટર્સ ફોર ડિસેઝ કંટ્રોલ અને પ્રીવેન્શન (CDC) અને નેશનલ ઇન્સ્ટીટ્યૂટ્સ ઓફ હેલ્થ (NIH) એ કોવિડ-19 માટે હાઇડ્રોક્સીક્લોર્ક્વિનનો પ્રાથમિક અથવા ઉપચાર માટે સલાહ આપી નથી આપી, કેટલાક ક્લિનિકલ પરીક્ષણ બાદ. ઔષધિ રોગના અધિકૃત ઉપચાર માર્ગદર્શિકાઓમાં સામેલ નથી.

સાંસદની સમાપ્તિ પછી, મોટા યુનાઇટેડ સ્ટેટ્સ સ્વાસ્થ્ય એજન્સીઓએ કોવિડ-19 માટે હાઇડ્રોક્સીક્લોર્ક્વિનનો અધિકૃત ઉપચાર તરીકે કોઈ પુનઃસ્થાપન અથવા નવા સમર્થન નથી કર્યો. છતાં કેટલાક વ્યક્તિગત ચિકિત્સકો અને પ્રોત્સાહન સમૂહો એ ઉપયોગની સલાહ આપતા રહે છે, પરંતુ આ માન્યતાઓ અધિકૃત યુનાઇટેડ સ્ટેટ્સ નીતિઓને પ્રતિબિંબિત કરતી નથી. વર્તમાન ફેડરલ માર્ગદર્શિકાઓ પેશેન્ટ યોગ્યતા અને રોગના તબક્કા પર આધાર રાખીને એન્ટિવિરલ ઔષધિઓ (ઉદાહરણ તરીકે, Paxlovid) અને મોનોક્લોનલ એન્ટીબોડીઓનો ઉપયોગ પ્રાથમિકતા આપે છે.

સારાંશમાં, "યુનાઇટેડ સ્ટેટ્સ એ કોવિડ-19 સામે હાઇડ્રોક્સીક્લોર્ક્વિનની અધિકૃત સલાહ આપી છે" આ દાવો અસાચો છે. FDA, CDC અને NIH સહિત ફેડરલ એજન્સીઓ કોવિડ-19 માટે હાઇડ્રોક્સીક્લોર્ક્વિનનો પ્રાથમિક અથવા ઉપચાર માટે સલાહ આપતી નથી. અધિકૃત માર્ગદર્શિકા વિસ્તૃત વિજ્ઞાનિક અધ્યયન પર આધારિત છે, જે ઔષધિને આ ઉદ્દેશે અસરકારક નથી અને સંભવિત ક્ષતિ પણ છે. હાલમાં, હાઇડ્રોક્સીક્લોર્ક્વિન કોવિડ-19 ઉપચાર માટે અનુમતિ મળેલા ક્લિનિકલ પરીક્ષણના કન્ટેક્ટમાં માત્ર ઉપયોગ કરવો જોઈએ.

Claims regarding adverse reactions to COVID-19 vaccines have circulated widely on social media since vaccination campaigns began. A recent post features photographs of two nurses, alleging that both experienced severe adverse reactions to COVID-19 vaccines and required hospital admission. Such claims can prompt significant concern, particularly among healthcare workers and members of the public considering vaccination. To assess the accuracy of this post, it is essential to review the context, examine the available evidence about vaccine safety, and investigate the origins and content of the images used.

COVID-19 vaccines underwent rigorous clinical trials before approval and have been administered to billions worldwide. Like all vaccines and medications, they can cause side effects. Most reported side effects are mild and short-lived, such as soreness at the injection site, fatigue, or mild fever. Rarely, serious reactions can occur, including allergic responses or other complications. Health authorities have systems in place to monitor and investigate these rare events.

The post in question claims that two nurses suffered severe reactions and were hospitalized. Such specific claims require careful scrutiny. In many cases, social media posts featuring alarming images are either misattributed, lack context, or are based on anecdotal evidence rather than verified medical reports. There have been documented cases where images of individuals in hospital settings have been repurposed or taken out of context to promote vaccine misinformation.

To verify the claim, a reverse image search was performed on the photographs circulating in the post. The results indicate that the images have been previously used in unrelated news stories and do not directly support the assertion that these specific individuals experienced severe vaccine reactions. Additionally, neither the post nor any identifiable news sources provide verifiable details such as names, dates, hospital admission records, or official statements from medical institutions to corroborate the story. Official health agencies have not reported widespread incidents of nurses or healthcare workers requiring hospitalization due to severe vaccine reactions.

It is important to recognize that while severe adverse events can occur, they are extremely rare and are closely monitored by health authorities. The benefit-risk profile of COVID-19 vaccines remains overwhelmingly positive, as vaccination significantly reduces the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death from the virus. Healthcare workers were among the first groups to receive vaccines, and while some experienced side effects, the vast majority reported only mild, temporary symptoms.

In summary, the claim that two nurses suffered severe reactions to COVID-19 vaccines and were hospitalized, as depicted in the shared photographs, lacks verifiable evidence. The images appear to be misrepresented, and no credible sources confirm the story. While rare adverse reactions can occur, current data and monitoring efforts indicate that such events are uncommon, and the overall safety profile of COVID-19 vaccines remains strong. It is vital for individuals to seek information from trusted health authorities and to approach unverified social media claims with skepticism.

article_content:
A recent social media post claims that researchers at the University of Liverpool have proven that ivermectin reduces COVID-19 deaths by 75% when administered early. This assertion has gained traction online, prompting widespread discussion and calls for the use of ivermectin as a COVID-19 treatment. A careful review of available evidence and the context surrounding ivermectin’s study is necessary to assess the accuracy of this claim.

Ivermectin is an antiparasitic drug long approved for treating conditions such as river blindness and scabies. During the COVID-19 pandemic, it came under investigation for its potential antiviral properties, leading to numerous studies worldwide. Some early laboratory research suggested ivermectin could inhibit replication of the coronavirus in cell cultures, but results in human trials have been inconsistent.

The University of Liverpool is among several institutions that have reviewed ivermectin research. Scholars from the university have contributed to meta-analyses and commentaries on the effectiveness of repurposed drugs for COVID-19, including ivermectin. One prominent meta-analysis led by researchers affiliated with the university assessed results from multiple trials, seeking to determine whether ivermectin impacts mortality and recovery rates when administered to COVID-19 patients.

The social media post references a 75% reduction in COVID-19 deaths with early ivermectin administration, purportedly “proven” by University of Liverpool researchers. However, the term “proven” implies a level of certainty and scientific consensus that does not exist with current ivermectin research. While some early studies and aggregated data suggested possible reductions in mortality with ivermectin, these findings were often limited by small sample sizes, methodological flaws, and the inclusion of non-peer-reviewed studies. Notably, several studies evaluating ivermectin’s efficacy were later retracted or found to contain significant errors, undermining the reliability of initial positive results.

University of Liverpool researchers have not released definitive clinical trial data proving that ivermectin reduces COVID-19 deaths by 75%. Instead, their meta-analyses have emphasized the need for cautious interpretation of available data, highlighting the risk of bias and the limitations of existing studies. They have called for rigorous, large-scale clinical trials to establish the drug’s true efficacy and safety profile before making any public health recommendations.

Major health authorities, including the World Health Organization and national regulatory agencies, have reviewed the evidence on ivermectin for COVID-19. To date, they have concluded that there is insufficient high-quality evidence to recommend ivermectin for the treatment or prevention of COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. These positions are informed by the variable results of studies and concerns over data integrity.

In summary, the claim that University of Liverpool researchers have proven ivermectin reduces COVID-19 deaths by 75% if administered early is misleading. While some research affiliated with the university has explored ivermectin’s potential, it has not established definitive proof of such a dramatic reduction in mortality. In early 2021, as Brazil grappled with the initial rollout of COVID-19 vaccines, an unusual incident captured national attention: reports emerged that a young man in Jaraguá do Sul, Santa Catarina, disguised himself as an elderly person to receive a vaccination ahead of his turn. This claim, which quickly spread on social media, prompted widespread discussion about vaccine prioritization, ethical conduct, and the challenges faced by public health officials during the unprecedented immunization campaign.

The core of the allegation is that a young individual, not yet eligible under the governmental prioritization guidelines, resorted to using makeup, prosthetics, or other means to alter his appearance. The intent, reportedly, was to deceive vaccination staff at a local health post into believing he was an elderly man, thus qualifying for early access. At the time, Santa Catarina, like the rest of Brazil, was distributing vaccines primarily to high-risk groups, including the elderly and healthcare workers. Many younger adults, anxious about the slow pace of vaccine rollout and the ongoing threat of COVID-19, faced long waits before their categories would become eligible.

Upon investigation, authorities in Jaraguá do Sul confirmed that a young man did indeed attempt to receive a vaccine by presenting himself as a senior citizen. Reports indicated that health workers became suspicious due to inconsistencies in the man’s appearance and documentation. It was alleged that he wore a wig, used heavy makeup, and donned clothing associated with older adults. Staff noticed discrepancies during the identification process, prompting closer scrutiny. Ultimately, the ruse was uncovered, and the individual was prevented from being vaccinated. Local police were notified, and the case was referred for further investigation to determine whether any legal consequences would follow.

This incident was not isolated at the national level. Across Brazil, several cases of individuals attempting to jump the vaccine queue were reported, ranging from the submission of false documentation to impersonation. These actions were widely condemned by health authorities and the public alike, as they undermined the integrity of the vaccination process and potentially put vulnerable populations at greater risk.

The episode in Jaraguá do Sul highlights both the desperation felt by some members of the public and the critical importance of robust verification measures at vaccination sites. Health officials responded by reaffirming the need for strict adherence to identification protocols, reminding the community that jumping the queue was not only unethical but could also be subject to legal penalties.

In conclusion, the core claim made in the social media post—that a young man used an old man’s disguise to attempt to get vaccinated in Jaraguá do Sul, Santa Catarina—is accurate. The attempt was thwarted by vigilant health workers, and authorities took appropriate action. The incident serves as a reminder of the challenges faced during mass vaccination campaigns and the necessity for vigilance and fairness in public health initiatives.

Кључни алат је да је млади особа, која је у то време била неодобрена у прописима за приоритет, користила боје, протезе или друге средства за промену изгледа. Циљ, према извештајима, био је да подвргне вакцинским службеницима у локалној здравственој појединици мислију да је старији човек, тако да би имао приступ пре него што је његова категорија била одобрена. Многи млади особи, узбунjeni спорим ритмом распореда вакцина и настојећи да се избегне угроза од коронавируса, изгледали су дужи очекивања пре него што је њихова категорија била одобрена.

После инспекције, службе у Жарагуа-до-Сул су потврдили да је млади особа стварно покушавала да добије вакцину представљајући се као старији човек. Извештаји су указивали да су здравствени радници били сумњиви због несагласности у изгледу и документацији особе. Намештају се да је носио косу, користио је тешке боје и облеко повезано са старијим особама. Службеници су забележили несагласности током процеса идентификације, што је довело до посебног прегледа. На крају, измештај је открићен, а особа је пресечена да добије вакцину. Локална полиција је информисана, а случај је упућен за додатну инспекцију да би се одредило да ли је било јавно последица.

Овај случај није био изолован на националном нивоу. По целини Бразила су извештавани случајеви где су особе покушавале да прескоче ред за вакцинацију, од праћења лажних документа до присуства. Случај у Жарагуа-до-Сул подсећа на оптужбу коју су неки чланови друштва осетили и важност строгих мера верификације на местима вакцинације. Здравствени службеници су одговорили потврдом потребе строге праћења протокола идентификације, напомињући заједници да прескакање реда није само неетички, већ могуће и подложно правно последицама.

У закључку, кључна тврдња на социјалним мрежама – да је млади човек користио изглед старијег особа да би покушао да добије вакцину у Жарагуа-до-Сул, у Сантакатарини – је тачна. Покушај је пресечен пажљивим здравственим радницима, а службе су узело одговорна мера. Случај служи као напомена о изазовима током масовних кампања за вакцинацију и неопходности пажње и правде у публичним здравственим иницијативама.

This assertion has sparked debate and confusion among her fans and the general public, raising questions about vaccine recommendations for people perceived to have strong immune systems.

Angélica, whose full name is Angélica Ksyvickis, is a prominent figure in Brazilian media, recognized for her decades-long career as a television host and actress. She is married to fellow TV presenter Luciano Huck, and the couple is often in the public eye. First, there are currently no verified interviews, official statements, or public appearances in which Angélica has declared she will refuse the COVID-19 vaccine due to having "high immunity." In fact, during the pandemic, many Brazilian celebrities used their platforms to encourage vaccination and share their experiences with COVID-19. If Angélica had made such a statement, it would likely have been widely reported by reputable news outlets, given her prominence. As of now, there is no substantiated evidence supporting the claim that Angélica refused vaccination for this reason.

The concept of "high immunity" as a rationale for declining vaccination is also not supported by medical science. COVID-19 vaccines are recommended for nearly all adults, regardless of perceived immune strength, except in rare cases of specific medical contraindications. The rationale is that even individuals who consider themselves healthy or immune-strong can contract and transmit the virus. Vaccination not only protects the individual from severe illness but also contributes to community immunity, reducing the overall spread of the virus.

Furthermore, public health agencies globally have emphasized that natural immunity or a strong immune system does not provide the same level of consistent protection as vaccination, especially against emerging variants of the virus. Vaccines are designed to boost and train the immune system to recognize and fight the virus more effectively.

In summary, there is no credible evidence that Angélica has refused the COVID-19 vaccine on the grounds of having "high immunity." The claim circulating on social media appears to be unfounded and does not align with known facts or established public health guidance. For accurate and up-to-date information on COVID-19 vaccination, individuals should consult official sources and medical professionals. Public figures like Angélica play an important role in influencing public opinion, making it essential to verify statements attributed to them before sharing or acting upon them.

A recent social media post claims that João Doria, then governor of São Paulo, announced that children would be vaccinated against COVID-19 in schools starting in February, even though the Coronavac vaccine is not recommended for this age group. This post has generated concern and confusion among parents and the public regarding the safety and approval status of the Coronavac vaccine for children.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to understand the context of COVID-19 vaccination efforts in São Paulo and Brazil, the approval process for vaccines, and official recommendations regarding pediatric vaccination.

**Context and Background**

João Doria, as governor of São Paulo, was a prominent figure in Brazil’s COVID-19 response. Under his leadership, São Paulo partnered with the Butantan Institute to produce Coronavac, a vaccine developed by Chinese pharmaceutical company Sinovac. Coronavac became one of the first vaccines available in Brazil, initially approved for use in adults.

As the pandemic evolved, authorities began to consider vaccinating younger populations to curb the spread of the virus and reduce severe cases. In late 2021 and early 2022, health authorities in several countries, including Brazil, evaluated the safety and efficacy of various vaccines for children.

**Coronavac Approval for Children**

At the time of the social media post, Coronavac’s use in children was a topic of active discussion. In January 2022, Brazil’s National Health Surveillance Agency (Anvisa) authorized the emergency use of Coronavac for children and adolescents aged 6 to 17 years, with the exception of immunocompromised individuals. This decision followed a review of safety and efficacy data submitted by the Butantan Institute.

Prior to this authorization, Coronavac was not recommended for children, which may explain lingering confusion and the basis for the claim in the social media post. However, as of the time of the planned school-based vaccination campaign in São Paulo, Coronavac had received official approval for use in the specified pediatric age group.

**Analysis of the Claim**

The social media post contains a mix of accurate and outdated information:

- It is accurate that João Doria publicly supported and promoted the vaccination of children in schools, with a planned start in February, in alignment with the school calendar.
- The claim that Coronavac is "not recommended for this age group" was true prior to Anvisa’s January 2022 authorization, but became outdated once the agency gave its approval for use in children aged 6 to 17.
- The school-based vaccination campaign was designed to use only vaccines approved by Anvisa for the relevant age groups, including Coronavac for children 6 and older, and Pfizer’s pediatric vaccine for ages 5 to 11.

**Conclusion**

The claim that children would be vaccinated in schools with Coronavac “even though the vaccine is not recommended for this age group” is misleading. At the time of the planned campaign, Coronavac had been authorized by Brazilian health authorities for use in children aged 6 to 17. The vaccination initiative in São Paulo schools adhered to these recommendations. While concerns about vaccine approval for children were valid prior to January 2022, the situation changed following Anvisa’s decision, and Coronavac was considered appropriate for the specified age group.

Om de nauwkeurigheid van deze bewering te beoordelen, is het belangrijk om de context van de vaccinatieinspanningen in São Paulo en Brazilië, de toestemmingstelling van vaccins en de officiële aanbevelingen betreffende kindervaccinatie te begrijpen.

**Context en achtergrond**

João Doria was als gouverneur van São Paulo een prominente figuur in Braziliës reactie op het coronavirus. Onder zijn leiding werkte São Paulo samen met het Butantan Instituut om Coronavac te produceren, een vaccine ontwikkeld door het Chinese farmaceutische bedrijf Sinovac. Coronavac werd een van de eerste vaccins beschikbaar in Brazilië en werd in eerste instantie toegestaan voor gebruik bij volwassenen.

Terwijl de pandemie zich ontwikkelde, begonnen autoriteiten overwegen om jongere bevolkingsgroepen te vaccineren om de verspreiding van het virus te beperken en ernstige gevallen te verminderen. In de late 2021 en vroege 2022 beoordeelden gezondheidsautoriteiten in verschillende landen, waaronder Brazilië, de veiligheid en effectiviteit van verschillende vaccins voor kinderen.

**Toestemming van Coronavac voor kinderen**

Op het moment van de sociale media-post was het gebruik van Coronavac bij kinderen een actief onderwerp van discussie. In januari 2022 gaf de Nationale Gezondheidsbewaking (Anvisa) toestemming voor het noodgebruik van Coronavac voor kinderen en jongeren van 6 tot 17 jaar, met uitzondering van immuunverzwakte personen. Deze beslissing volgde op een beoordeling van veiligheids- en effectiviteitsdata die het Butantan Instituut had ingezonden.

Voor deze toestemming was Coronavac niet aanbevolen voor kinderen, wat mogelijk de oorzaak is van de blijvende verwarring en de basis van de bewering in de sociale media-post. Echter, op het moment van de geplande schoolgebonden vaccinatiecampagne in São Paulo had Coronavac officiële toestemming voor gebruik in de aangegeven kinderleeftijdsgroep.

**Analyse van de bewering**

De sociale media-post bevat een mengeling van nauwkeurige en verouderde informatie:

- Het is correct dat João Doria openlijk steun gaf en promootte voor de vaccinatie van kinderen in de scholen, met een geplande start in februari, in overeenstemming met het schooljaar.
- De bewering dat Coronavac "niet aanbevolen is voor deze leeftijdsgroep" was waar voor Anvisas toestemming in januari 2022, maar werd verouderd toen de autoriteit toestemming gaf voor gebruik bij kinderen van 6 tot 17 jaar.
- De schoolgebonden vaccinatiecampagne was ontworpen om alleen vaccins te gebruiken die toegestaan waren door Anvisa voor de relevante leeftijdsgroepen, waaronder Coronavac voor kinderen van 6 jaar en ouder en de pediatrische Pfizer-vaccinatie voor kinderen van 5 tot 11 jaar.

**Conclusie**

De bewering dat kinderen in de scholen gevaccineerd zouden worden met Coronavac "ondanks dat het vaccin niet aanbevolen is voor deze leeftijdsgroep" is misleidend. Op het moment van de geplande campagne had Coronavac toestemming van de Braziliaanse gezondheidsautoriteiten voor gebruik bij kinderen van 6 tot 17 jaar. De vaccinatieinitiatief in de scholen van São Paulo volgde deze aanbevelingen. Hoewel zorgen over de toestemming van vaccins voor kinderen geldig waren voorafgaand aan januari 2022, veranderde de situatie na de beslissing van Anvisa, en werd Coronavac beschouwd als geschikt voor de aangegeven leeftijdsgroep.

article_content:
A widely circulated audio recording on social media has sparked concern by alleging that an Australian COVID-19 vaccine infected recipients with HIV. The audio, which has gained traction among conspiracy theory circles, makes a series of alarming claims, the most serious being that a vaccine developed in Australia was responsible for transmitting HIV to people who received it. This article examines the origins of this claim, the facts surrounding the vaccine in question, and the broader context of vaccine development and safety monitoring.

The claim centers on a COVID-19 vaccine candidate developed by the University of Queensland in partnership with biotechnology company CSL Limited. In late 2020, this vaccine was part of Australia’s strategy to develop multiple options in the fight against COVID-19. However, during clinical trials, some participants returned false-positive results in HIV tests. This was due to a component of the vaccine's design: the use of a small fragment of a protein derived from HIV. This fragment was used solely as a molecular "clamp" to stabilize the vaccine's spike protein, making it more effective at provoking an immune response.

It is essential to clarify that the fragment used in the vaccine could not cause HIV infection. The protein segment was not infectious and did not contain any functional parts of the HIV virus. Its only effect was to trigger an immune response that, in some cases, led to false-positive results on certain HIV tests. Upon identifying this issue, the clinical trial was halted, and the vaccine was withdrawn from further development. Australian health authorities and the developers made this information public and emphasized that there was no risk of HIV infection from the vaccine.

At no point did the vaccine transmit HIV or cause HIV infection in recipients. The decision to discontinue the vaccine was based on the potential for confusion and public concern over false-positive HIV test results, not on any actual cases of HIV infection. Further, extensive testing and monitoring of trial participants confirmed that no one had contracted HIV as a result of receiving the vaccine.

Conspiracy theories like the one featured in the audio recording often capitalize on scientific misunderstandings and public fears. In this case, the presence of an HIV protein fragment — a common tool in vaccine research — was misinterpreted and misrepresented as evidence of deliberate or accidental HIV transmission. However, the clinical and regulatory processes in place for vaccine development are designed to identify and address such issues before a product is approved for widespread use.

In summary, the claim that an Australian COVID-19 vaccine infected people with HIV is false. While the vaccine candidate did cause some false-positive results on HIV tests, it did not contain any infectious HIV material and posed no risk of transmitting the virus. The episode underscores the importance of transparent communication in public health and the need to critically evaluate sources of information circulating on social media.

In January 2021, amid a severe COVID-19 surge, the city of Manaus in Brazil faced a dire shortage of medical oxygen, leading to a humanitarian crisis in its hospitals. Reports of patients dying from asphyxiation due to lack of oxygen prompted urgent calls for assistance both domestically and internationally. In response, the Venezuelan government announced that it had donated oxygen to Manaus, presenting this gesture as humanitarian solidarity with its neighboring country. However, questions have arisen regarding the veracity of this claim, with allegations that the oxygen delivered was not a government donation but rather a commercial import facilitated by the private company White Martins.

To assess the accuracy of the social media claim—that the Venezuelan government “lied” about donating oxygen and that the supply was actually imported by White Martins—it is essential to examine the documented events and the roles of the involved parties.

White Martins is a leading supplier of industrial and medical gases in Brazil and operates as a subsidiary of multinational Linde plc. The company has longstanding logistical networks for importing and distributing oxygen, including cross-border arrangements. During the Manaus crisis, White Martins was under immense pressure to ramp up oxygen deliveries to the region. Given the urgency and proximity, Venezuela was identified as a potential source for liquid oxygen supplies.

According to reports at the time, White Martins negotiated the purchase and transport of oxygen from Venezuela to Manaus. Trucks carrying oxygen crossed the border, and the company coordinated with Brazilian authorities to expedite the process. While the Venezuelan government publicly framed the shipment as a donation, evidence suggests that the oxygen was procured through commercial channels by White Martins and not directly gifted by the state. This distinction is crucial, as a donation would imply that the Venezuelan government absorbed the costs and initiated the shipment for humanitarian reasons, rather than responding to a business transaction.

The Venezuelan government’s narrative likely served political and diplomatic purposes, showcasing its willingness to help a neighbor in crisis. However, logistical details provided by White Martins and corroborated by Brazilian officials indicate that the supply chain followed standard import procedures, with payment arrangements in place and no clear evidence of a government-funded donation. Furthermore, the oxygen was delivered directly to White Martins facilities and distributed through their existing infrastructure, not through government-to-government channels.

This analysis supports the core claim made in the social media post: the oxygen that arrived in Manaus from Venezuela during the COVID-19 emergency was not a direct donation from the Venezuelan government, but rather a commercial import coordinated and paid for by White Martins. The Venezuelan government’s statements misrepresented the nature of the assistance, conflating commercial transactions with humanitarian aid.

In summary, while oxygen from Venezuela played a critical role in alleviating the Manaus crisis, the available evidence indicates that the Venezuelan government did not donate the oxygen as claimed. Instead, the supply was imported by White Martins, a private company, in accordance with established business practices. The Venezuelan government’s portrayal of the shipment as a donation was misleading, and the social media post’s core assertion is supported by the documented facts.

Bu durum, hem ulusal hem de uluslararası düzeyde yardım çağrısı doğurdu. Venezuelalı hükümet, Manaus'a oksijen bağışlamış olmaktan duyduğu memnuniyeti dile getirerek bu tutumu komşu ülkeye yönelik insani dayanışma olarak açıkladı. Sosyal medya üzerinde "Venezuela hükümetinin oksijen bağışlamadığını" ve oksijenin aslında White Martins tarafından ithal edildiğini iddia eden bir tweetin doğruluğunu değerlendirmek için olayların belgeli hali ve ilgili tarafların rolleri incelenmelidir.

White Martins, Brezilya'da endüstriyel ve tıbbi gazların önde gelen satıcısıdır ve uluslararası şirket Linde plc'nin bir yan kuruluşudur. Şirket, oksijenin ithal edilmesi ve dağıtımında uzun yıllar boyunca logistik ağları ve kara sınırlar arası anlaşmaları vardır. Manaus krizi sırasında, oksijen sevkiyatlarını bölgeye artırmak için baskı altına alınmıştır. Aciliyet ve yakınlık nedeniyle Venezuela, sıvı oksijen kaynakları olarak değerlendirilmiştir.

Olayların o dönemki bildirimlerine göre, White Martins Venezuela'dan Manaus'a oksijenin satın alınması ve taşınması için müzakereler yapmıştır. Oksijen taşıyan kamyonlar sınırı geçerek seyahat etmiş ve şirket, Brezilya yetkilileriyle koordinasyon sağlayarak süreci hızlandırmıştır. Venezuela hükümeti, bu sevkiyatı bağış olarak açıklarken, kanıt göstermektedir ki oksijen White Martins tarafından ticari kanallar aracılığıyla temin edilmiştir ve devletin doğrudan bağışladığı değil. Bu ayrım çok önemlidir çünkü bağış olarak ifade edilmesi, Venezuela hükümetinin maliyeti kendi üzerine alarak insani amaçlar doğrultusunda sevkiyatı gerçekleştirmiş olmasının ima ederken, ticari bir işlem olduğuna dair kanıt yoktur.

Venezuela hükümetinin anlatımı, muhtemelen siyasi ve diplomatik amaçlarla ilişkilidir. Ancak White Martins tarafından verilen logistik detaylar ve Brezilya yetkilileri tarafından desteklenen bu bilgiler, oksijenin normal ithal prosedürlerine göre sevkiyat yapıldığını ve ödeme düzenlemeleri olduğu, devlet tarafından finanse edilen bir bağış olmadığına işaret etmektedir. Ayrıca, oksijen, Venezuela hükümeti ile devlet düzeyindeki bir anlaşmazlık olmadan, doğrudan White Martins tesislerine teslim edilmiş ve mevcut altyapı aracılığıyla dağıtılmıştır.

Bu analiz, sosyal medya paylaşımlarında yapılan temel iddianın doğruluğunu desteklemektedir: COVID-19 acil durumu sırasında Venezuela'dan Manaus'a gelen oksijen, Venezuela hükümetinin doğrudan bağışladığı değil, White Martins adlı özel bir şirket tarafından ticari olarak ithal edilmiştir. Venezuela hükümetinin açıklamaları, ticari işlemlerle insani yardım arasında karışıklık yaratmış ve sosyal medya paylaşımlarında yapılan temel iddia, belgeli bilgilerle desteklenmektedir.

Özetle, Venezuela'dan gelen oksijen, Manaus krizini gidermek için kritik bir rol oynamış olsa da, mevcut kanıtlar, Venezuela hükümetinin oksijeni bağışladığını iddia ettiğini göstermektedir. Bunun yerine, oksijen, özel şirket White Martins tarafından ticari yöntemlerle ithal edilmiştir. Venezuela hükümeti tarafından yapılan açıklamalar, sevkiyatın bağış olduğunu ifade etmekle yanıltıcıdır ve sosyal medya paylaşımlarında yapılan temel iddia belgeli bilgilerle desteklenmektedir.

In January 2021, Monica Calazans, a nurse from São Paulo, became a symbol of hope for Brazil when she received the country’s first publicly administered COVID-19 vaccine dose during a widely broadcast ceremony. Her vaccination marked the official start of Brazil’s national immunization campaign against COVID-19, using the CoronaVac vaccine, developed by Sinovac and produced locally by the Butantan Institute.

A claim circulating on social media suggests Monica Calazans had already received the vaccine prior to this historic event, as she was a participant in the clinical trials for CoronaVac. This assertion raises questions about the authenticity of the event and whether she was, in fact, the "first" person in Brazil to be vaccinated against COVID-19.

To examine the validity of this claim, it is important to understand the vaccine trial process and Monica Calazans's participation. Clinical trials for vaccines typically involve thousands of volunteers, some of whom receive the experimental vaccine, while others receive a placebo. The CoronaVac trials in Brazil began months before the public vaccination campaign, enrolling healthcare workers, including nurses like Calazans, who were at high risk of exposure to COVID-19.

Monica Calazans was indeed a frontline nurse and a participant in the CoronaVac clinical trials. However, participation in a trial does not guarantee that a volunteer receives the actual vaccine; some receive a placebo as part of the study’s design. Furthermore, trial participants are generally not informed of their group assignment during the study. In Calazans's case, there is no publicly available evidence confirming whether she received the vaccine or the placebo during the clinical trial phase.

The ceremonial vaccination in January 2021 was intended to mark the beginning of the national rollout, using officially approved doses of CoronaVac. The event was broadcast live and attended by government officials, with Calazans chosen for both her frontline status and her representation of the vulnerable population. Her vaccination was the first to be administered outside of the clinical trial setting, using doses earmarked for the general public.

It is also essential to note that clinical trial vaccinations differ significantly from official public immunizations. The former is part of an experimental protocol, subject to strict monitoring and data collection, and does not confer the same status as receiving an approved vaccine through a national program. The first person to be vaccinated in a clinical trial is not recognized as the first to be vaccinated in a public campaign.

In conclusion, while Monica Calazans was a participant in the CoronaVac trials, there is no evidence she received the vaccine as part of that process prior to her public immunization. Her televised vaccination was the first official, approved COVID-19 vaccine administered in Brazil's nationwide campaign. The social media claim oversimplifies and misrepresents the distinction between clinical trial participation and public vaccination. Monica Calazans remains the first person in Brazil to receive a COVID-19 vaccine dose as part of the country’s official campaign, regardless of her prior involvement in vaccine studies.

ਜਨਵਰੀ 2021 ਵਿੱਚ, ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ, ਸਾਂ ਪੇਲੋ ਦੀ ਇੱਕ ਚੀਨੀ, ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਪ੍ਰਥਮ ਸਾਂਖੀ ਸੇਵਾ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਜਨਤਾ ਦੇ ਮੁਕਾਬਲੇ ਵਿੱਚ ਇੱਕ ਸੰਖੇਪ ਸੰਕੇਤ ਦੇ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਹੋਈ ਹੈ, ਜਿਸ ਨੂੰ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਲਈ ਇੱਕ ਵਿਸ਼ਾਲ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਦੇ ਰਾਸ਼ਟਰੀ ਵੈਕਸੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਕੈਂਪੇਨ ਦੇ ਆਖਰੀ ਕਦਮ ਦੇ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਮੰਨਿਆ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ। ਇਸ ਕਦਮ ਨੇ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਦੇ ਰਾਸ਼ਟਰੀ ਵੈਕਸੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਕੈਂਪੇਨ ਦੇ ਆਖਰੀ ਕਦਮ ਨੂੰ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤ ਦੇ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਮੰਨਿਆ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ, ਜੋ ਸਿਨੋਵੈਕ ਦੁਆਰਾ ਵਿਕਸਿਤ ਅਤੇ ਬੁਟੈਂਟਾਨ ਸੰਸਥਾ ਦੁਆਰਾ ਬਣਾਇਆ ਗਿਆ ਹੈ।

ਸਮਾਜੀ ਮੀਡੀਆ 'ਤੇ ਚਲ ਰਹੇ ਇੱਕ ਦਾਅਵਾ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਇਸ ਐਤਵਾਰੀ ਘਟਨਾ ਤੋਂ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਹੀ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰ ਚੁੱਕੀ ਸੀ, ਕਿਉਂਕਿ ਉਸਨੇ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਦੇ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗ ਲੈਣ ਵਾਲੀ ਵਿਅਕਤੀ ਸੀ। ਇਸ ਦਾਅਵੇ ਘਟਨਾ ਦੀ ਸਹੀਤਾ ਬਾਰੇ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਨ ਉਠਾਉਂਦਾ ਹੈ ਅਤੇ ਇਸ ਦੀ ਬਾਰੇ ਇਹ ਪੁੱਛਦਾ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਕੀ ਵਾਸਤਵਿਕ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਉਸਨੂੰ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵਿਰੁੱਧ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੀ ਪਹਿਲੀ ਵਿਅਕਤੀ ਸੀ।

ਇਸ ਦਾਅਵੇ ਦੀ ਸਹੀਤਾ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ ਇਸ ਗੱਲ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ ਕਰਨੀ ਜਰੂਰੀ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਪ੍ਰਕਿਰਿਆ ਅਤੇ ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਦੀ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰੀ ਦੀ ਗੱਲ ਕੀਤੀ ਜਾਵੇ। ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਆਮ ਤੌਰ 'ਤੇ ਹਜ਼ਾਰਾਂ ਸੰਸ਼ੋਧਨ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੇ ਵਿਅਕਤੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਮੂਲੀਅਤ ਦੀ ਸੂਚੀ ਹੁੰਦੀ ਹੈ, ਜਿਨ੍ਹਾਂ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੁਝ ਵਿਅਕਤੀਆਂ ਨੂੰ ਅਧਿਐਨ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਅਤੇ ਕੁਝ ਨੂੰ ਪਲੇਸੀਬੋ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਸੰਸ਼ੋਧਨ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੇ ਹੁੰਦੇ ਹਨ। ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਪ੍ਰਕਿਰਿਆ ਪਬਲਿਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਕੈਂਪੇਨ ਤੋਂ ਮਹੀਨਾ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਸ਼ੁਰੂ ਹੋ ਗਈ ਸੀ, ਜਿਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਸਿਹਤ ਕਰਮੀਆਂ ਨੂੰ ਸ਼ਾਮਲ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਸੀ, ਜਿਨ੍ਹਾਂ ਵਿੱਚ ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਵਰਗੇ ਨਰਸਾਂ ਵੀ ਸ਼ਾਮਲ ਹਨ, ਜੋ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵਿਰੁੱਧ ਕੰਮ ਕਰਨ ਦੇ ਖ਼ਾਸ ਖ਼ਤਰੇ ਵਿੱਚ ਸਨ।

ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਵਿਸ਼ਵ ਸਿਰਜਣ ਨਰਸ ਅਤੇ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੀ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰ ਸੀ। ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੀ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰੀ ਨੂੰ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਦੀ ਗਾਰੰਟੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਦੇਂਦੀ, ਕਿਉਂਕਿ ਕੁਝ ਵਿਅਕਤੀਆਂ ਨੂੰ ਪਲੇਸੀਬੋ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਸੰਸ਼ੋਧਨ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੇ ਹੁੰਦੇ ਹਨ। ਇਸ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰ ਆਮ ਤੌਰ 'ਤੇ ਅਧਿਐਨ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਆਪਣੇ ਕੋਲ ਕਿਸ ਗਰੁੱਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਸ਼ਾਮਲ ਹੋਣ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ ਨਹੀਂ ਕਰਦੇ। ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਦੇ ਕੇਸ ਵਿੱਚ, ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਉਸਨੂੰ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਅਤੇ ਪਲੇਸੀਬੋ ਵਿੱਚੋਂ ਕਿਸੇ ਨੂੰ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਹੋਇਆ ਹੈ ਇਸ ਬਾਰੇ ਪ੍ਰਕਾਸ਼ਿਤ ਕੋਈ ਪ੍ਰਮਾਣ ਨਹੀਂ ਮਿਲਿਆ ਹੈ।

ਜਨਵਰੀ 2021 ਵਿੱਚ ਕੇਂਦਰੀ ਸੇਵਾ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਕੇਂਦਰੀ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤ ਦੇ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਇਸ ਕਦਮ ਦਾ ਮੁੱਖ ਉਦੇਸ਼ ਰਾਸ਼ਟਰੀ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਦੇ ਪਹਿਲੇ ਦੌਰ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਇਸ ਦੀ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤ ਕਰਨਾ ਸੀ। ਇਸ ਘਟਨਾ ਨੂੰ ਜੀਵਨ ਲੀਵ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਸੀ ਅਤੇ ਸਰਕਾਰੀ ਅਧਿਕਾਰੀਆਂ ਦੀ ਸ਼ਮੂਲੀਅਤ ਹੋਈ ਸੀ, ਜਿਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਦੀ ਚੂਹੜੀ ਵਿਸ਼ਵ ਸਿਰਜਣ ਅਤੇ ਨਾਟਕੀ ਸਮੁਦਾਇਕ ਵਰਗ ਦੀ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ੰਸ਼ਾ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ ਚੁਣਿਆ ਗਿਆ ਸੀ। ਉਸ ਦੀ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤੀ ਕੇਂਦਰੀ ਸੇਵਾ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਬਾਹਰ ਕੀਤੀ ਗਈ ਸੀ, ਜਿਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਸਾਮਾਨਿਆਂ ਲਈ ਵਰਤੇ ਗਏ ਡੋਜ਼ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਸੀ।

ਇਸ ਨੂੰ ਵੀ ਧਿਆਨ ਦੇਣਾ ਜ਼ਰੂਰੀ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤ ਅਤੇ ਆਖਰੀ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੱਖ-ਵੱਖ ਹੈ। ਪਹਿਲਾ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੀ ਵਿਅਕਤੀ ਕੋਈ ਵੀ ਆਖਰੀ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੀ ਪਹਿਲੀ ਵਿਅਕਤੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਮੰਨੀ ਜਾਂਦੀ।

ਅਤੇ ਸ਼ਾਮਲ ਹੈ, ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰ ਸੀ, ਪਰ ਕੋਈ ਪ੍ਰਮਾਣ ਨਹੀਂ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਉਸਨੇ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕੀਤੀ ਸੀ ਜੋ ਉਸਦੀ ਸਾਂਖੀ ਸੇਵਾ ਦੇ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਹੀ ਹੋਈ ਹੈ। ਉਸ ਦੀ ਟੈਲੀਵਿਜ਼ਨ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤੀ ਕੇਂਦਰੀ ਸੇਵਾ ਵਿੱਚ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਦੇ ਰਾਸ਼ਟਰੀ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਦੀ ਪਹਿਲੀ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਸੀ। ਸਮਾਜੀ ਮੀਡੀਆ ਦਾਅਵਾ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰੀ ਅਤੇ ਸਾਂਖੀ ਸੇਵਾ ਦੇ ਵਿਚਕਾਰ ਅੰਤਰ ਦਾ ਅਸਲੀ ਤੌਰ 'ਤੇ ਅਨੁਮਾਨ ਨਹੀਂ ਦਿੰਦਾ। ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਦੇ ਰਾਸ਼ਟਰੀ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਣ ਵਿੱਚ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਪਹਿਲੀ ਡੋਜ਼ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਵਾਲੀ ਵਿਅਕਤੀ ਹੈ, ਹਾਲਾਂ ਕਿ ਉਸਨੇ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗ ਲਿਆ ਸੀ।
article_summary: Monica Calazans, enfermeira de São Paulo, tornou-se símbolo de esperança ao ser a primeira pessoa a receber a vacina contra a COVID-19 em cerimônia pública no Brasil, em janeiro de 2021, marcando o início da campanha nacional com a CoronaVac. A recent social media post claims that the Department of Transit in Manaus will impound any car found on the city’s streets between 7pm and 5am as a measure to reduce the spread of COVID-19. This assertion has generated significant concern among residents, prompting questions about its accuracy and the current state of pandemic-related restrictions in Manaus, the capital of Brazil’s Amazonas state.

To evaluate the veracity of this claim, it is important to revisit the context of COVID-19 measures in Manaus. The city experienced severe outbreaks during the pandemic, leading authorities to adopt strict health and mobility measures at different times. These included curfews, restrictions on business operations, and limitations on public gatherings. Local law enforcement and transit authorities were at times involved in enforcing these rules to curb the spread of the virus.

The core claim— that the Department of Transit (Departamento de Trânsito) will impound any car on Manaus streets between 7pm and 5am— suggests an extreme enforcement measure akin to a blanket vehicle ban during nighttime hours. Such an action would mark a sharp escalation from previous traffic and mobility restrictions, which typically focused on limiting non-essential movement and enforcing curfews through fines or checkpoints, rather than automatic vehicle impoundment.

To determine the accuracy of the claim, it is necessary to examine official statements and recent policies from municipal authorities. As of the latest available information, the Manaus city government and the Department of Transit have not announced any policy mandating the impoundment of all vehicles on city streets during specified hours as a COVID-19 measure. Past curfews, when in place, were enforced primarily through police patrols and requests for justification of movement, particularly for essential workers. Vehicles were stopped and drivers asked to provide proof of essential work or valid reasons for being outside, but widespread impoundment was not a standard practice.

Additionally, as the COVID-19 situation has evolved, most cities in Brazil, including Manaus, have relaxed strict lockdown and curfew measures in response to vaccination campaigns and declining case numbers. While health recommendations and certain restrictions may remain, there is no current evidence of active, citywide vehicle impoundment policies tied to pandemic control.

It is also worth noting that misinformation regarding government enforcement actions has periodically circulated online, especially during times of crisis when anxiety and confusion are high. Such posts can inadvertently cause unnecessary alarm and may undermine trust in public health communications.

In summary, based on the current and historical actions of Manaus transit authorities, the claim that all cars will be impounded between 7pm and 5am as a COVID-19 measure is not substantiated by official policies or recent enforcement practices. Residents should consult verified channels for updates on public health measures and avoid spreading unverified information that could contribute to public confusion.

Nedavni post na društvenim mrežama tvrdi da će Odbor za promet u Manausu zaključati svako vozilo pronađeno na ulicama grada između 19 sati i 5 sati popodne kao mjera za smanjenje širenja kovida-19. Ova tvrdnja je izazvala značajnu zabrinutost među stanovnicima, što je dovelo do pitanja o njenom tačnosti i trenutnom stanju ograničenja vezanih za pandemiju u Manausu, glavnom gradu saveznog zavoda Amazonas.

Da bi se procijenila tačnost ovog tvrdnjenja, važno je ponoviti kontekst mjera protiv kovida-19 u Manausu. Grad je doživio ozbiljne izbore tokom pandemije, što je dovelo vlasti da su razvile stroge zdravstvene i mobilne mjere u različitim vremenima. Uključivala su se noćne zabrane, ograničenja radnog funkcionisanja poslova i ograničenja javnih skupova. Mjere su često izvršavale lokalne policije i službe za promet kako bi se smanjilo širenje virusa.

Ključna tvrdnja – da će Odbor za promet (Departamento de Trânsito) zaključati svako vozilo na ulicama Manausa između 19 sati i 5 sati popodne – predstavlja ekstremnu mjera izvršavanja sličnu potpunoj zabrani vozila tokom noćnih sati. Takvo ponašanje bi označavalo značajnu eskalaciju u odnosu na prethodne ograničenja u prometu i mobilnosti, koje su uglavnom bile usmjerene na smanjenje neophodnih aktivnosti i izvršavanje noćnih zabrana kroz kazne ili kontrolne točke, a ne kroz automatizovano zaključavanje vozila.

Da bi se utvrdila tačnost tvrdnje, potrebno je analizirati službene izjave i najnovije politike lokalnih vlasti. Prema najnovijim dostupnim informacijama, manauska općinska uprava i Odbor za promet nisu objavili nikakvu politiku koja zahtijeva zaključavanje svih vozila na ulicama grada tokom određenih sati kao mjera protiv kovida-19. Prethodne noćne zabrane, kada su bile u važećem stanju, izvršavale su se prema većini slučajeva putem patrulja policije i zahtjeva za objašnjenje mobilnosti, posebno za radnike u ključnim sektorima. Vozila su zadržavana i vozači su traženi da pruže dokaz o ključnom radu ili valjanoj razlogu za izlazak, ali je široko zaključavanje vozila bilo redovna praksa.

Takođe je važno napomenuti da se nepravilna informacija o izvršenju akcija stranih vlasti periodički širila putem interneta, posebno tokom krisa kada je zabrinutost i zabunica bili visoki. Takvi postovi mogu nezamjenjivo izazvati nepotrebu zabrinutost i mogu poduzeti poštenje javnih informacija o zdravstvenim preporukama.

U skladu s trenutnim i historijskim djelovanjem manauskog službenog prometnog uređaja, tvrdnja da će sve vozila biti zaključana između 19 sati i 5 sati popodne kao mjera protiv kovida-19 nije poduputa službenim politikama ili najnovijim izvršenim praksama. Stanovnici treba da se obrate verifikovanim izvorima za ažuriranja o zdravstvenim mjera i da izbjegavaju širenje neverifikovane informacije koja bi mogla doprinijeti javnoj zabunici.

In January 2021, Manaus, the capital city of Brazil’s Amazonas state, became the epicenter of a dire health crisis during the COVID-19 pandemic. Hospitals in the city ran critically low on medical oxygen, resulting in scenes of desperation as patients struggled to breathe while their families searched for oxygen cylinders. This crisis sparked widespread outrage and questions about how such a shortage could occur in one of Brazil’s largest cities.

A social media post recently circulated, claiming that White Martins, the leading supplier of medical oxygen in Manaus, refused to supply oxygen to public hospitals because the Amazonas state government owed them 52 million reais. Additionally, the post asserts that the government did not seek alternative suppliers because those companies were allegedly owned by political adversaries.

To assess the accuracy of these claims, it is important to understand the context and the facts surrounding the oxygen crisis.

White Martins is the primary provider of industrial and medical gases in Brazil, including the Amazonas region. The logistics of supplying this quantity of oxygen, especially given the remote location and limited infrastructure connecting Manaus to major production centers, presented enormous challenges.

Public records and news reports indicated that the debt reached tens of millions of reais, and White Martins had previously flagged these arrears to the authorities. The oxygen crisis in Manaus was a complex event, driven by overwhelming demand, logistical obstacles, and administrative challenges, with no clear evidence that the main supplier or state officials acted with deliberate malice.

A social media post has been circulating, showing a photograph of what appears to be a package of the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine with the label “made in China.” The implication is that Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccines are manufactured in China, a claim that has generated considerable discussion and confusion online. This article examines the veracity of this claim, providing context and a thorough fact-checking analysis.

The Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, marketed under the brand name Comirnaty, was developed jointly by Pfizer, an American pharmaceutical corporation, and BioNTech, a German biotechnology company. Since its emergency use authorization in late 2020, the vaccine has been produced and distributed globally, with manufacturing sites located in the United States, Germany, Belgium, and other countries.

The claim that Pfizer’s vaccine is manufactured in China has surfaced periodically, often accompanied by images purportedly showing vaccine packaging with Chinese manufacturing labels. To assess this claim, it is important to review Pfizer’s official manufacturing and distribution arrangements.

Pfizer has publicly listed its main vaccine production sites, which are located in Kalamazoo, Michigan (USA); Puurs (Belgium); and Mainz (Germany). In addition, Pfizer has contracted with several partner facilities in Europe and North America to meet global demand. There have been no official announcements or credible reports indicating that Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine for global distribution is manufactured in China.

However, in December 2021, Pfizer announced a partnership with Chinese pharmaceutical company Fosun Pharma to manufacture and distribute the Comirnaty vaccine within mainland China, Macau, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. Under this arrangement, Fosun Pharma handles local production and distribution for these markets. This means that some doses administered within these regions may be manufactured in China under Pfizer’s licensing agreement with Fosun Pharma. It is important to note that these doses are intended exclusively for the Chinese market and its territories, not for export to other countries.

The image in the social media post likely shows packaging for doses produced under this local partnership for the Chinese market. There is no evidence to suggest that Pfizer vaccines labeled “made in China” are being distributed outside of China, nor that vaccines for the United States, Europe, or other parts of the world are manufactured in China.

The broader context is that global vaccine production often involves complex partnerships and supply chains, especially during a pandemic. While Pfizer’s main production sites for most of the world are outside China, localized manufacturing under license is a common practice for serving specific markets and complying with local regulations.

In summary, the claim that all or most Pfizer vaccines are “made in China” is misleading. While Pfizer does have a partnership for local production in China for that market, the vast majority of vaccine doses distributed globally are manufactured in the United States and Europe. The image in question likely shows packaging for the Chinese market only, not a global production shift. As with all viral claims about vaccines, context and careful examination are vital to understanding the facts.
